## Proof

**Claim.** Let $S = \operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\dots,v_{n+1}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a full-dimensional simplex with centroid $v_c=\tfrac{1}{n+1}\sum_i v_i$. Then for every $v\in S$,
$$\|v-v_c\|_2 \;\le\; \max_{i=1,\dots,n+1}\|v_i-v_c\|_2.$$

**Proof.** Consider the function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by
$$f(x)=\|x-v_c\|_2^2 = (x-v_c)\cdot(x-v_c).$$
Its Hessian is $2I_n$, which is positive definite, so $f$ is **strictly convex** (in particular, convex).

The simplex $S$ is a compact convex set, and every point $v\in S$ has a unique representation as a convex combination of the vertices:
$$v=\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\lambda_i v_i,\qquad \lambda_i\ge 0,\quad \sum_i\lambda_i=1.$$

By convexity of $f$ (Jensen's inequality),
$$f(v)=f\!\Big(\sum_i\lambda_i v_i\Big)\;\le\;\sum_i\lambda_i\, f(v_i)\;\le\;\sum_i\lambda_i\Big(\max_j f(v_j)\Big)=\max_j f(v_j).$$
The last equality uses $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$. Hence
$$\|v-v_c\|_2^2 \;\le\; \max_{j}\|v_j-v_c\|_2^2.$$
Taking square roots (all quantities non-negative),
$$\|v-v_c\|_2 \;\le\; \max_{j}\|v_j-v_c\|_2.$$

**Remark (sharpness).** The bound is attained: choosing $v=v_k$ for any vertex gives $\|v_k-v_c\|_2\le\max_i\|v_i-v_c\|_2$ trivially, and at least one vertex realizes the maximum. So the inequality is tight and the right-hand side is exactly $\max_{v\in S}\|v-v_c\|_2$.

**Equivalent viewpoint.** Since a convex function on a compact convex polytope attains its maximum at an extreme point, and the extreme points of $S$ are precisely $v_1,\dots,v_{n+1}$, we have $\max_{v\in S}f(v)=\max_i f(v_i)$, which is the same conclusion.

Therefore the answer is **yes**: every point of the simplex lies within distance $\max_i\|v_i-v_c\|_2$ of the centroid. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
